groups.q: The narrator is nervous here. Does each line sound natural in your language?

rows.text: With trembling hands I flipped frantically through the ghazals, searching for the Hafez beit that, like the painting, as that other girl had said, would make us more shit-dizzy the deeper we sank into it.
rows.note: he repeats a crude word a girl made up about a painting

rows.text: Like that: the more you think about these ten words, the more sh— I mean, the dizzier you get.
rows.note: he almost says the crude word again, then stops

rows.text: For-for God's sake, listen. … It's like that painting your fr-fr-friend was showing you.
rows.note: he stammers

groups.q: The narrator finally tells the girl he loves her. Does it sound natural and heartfelt?

rows.text: I've loved you for thirty-two months. From a distance. Without your knowing. In silence, without a single word. You might say it's impossible: it can't be real; it's just fantasy. But it is real, and I truly love you.
rows.note: in Persian he speaks to her formally, with the polite 'you'

groups.q: These are the book's first lines. Do they read naturally and clearly?

rows.text: Here, nothing happens. Nothing will be set right, nothing torn down. No interpretation is coming. No conclusion.
This is the loose end of a thread of words that were once sounds.
As in childhood, when Maman would unravel the yarn of old clothes, and we would take the thread and walk around inside the house so the yarn would not pile up.
rows.note: Maman is Persian for 'mother', kept untranslated on purpose. The children carry the thread through the house as she unravels it.

rows.text: Now I unwind the thread of words, and you pick them up and carry them into your own world, so they will not pile up here, in my world.

groups.q: The memory comes loose like a screw with stripped threads. Is the image clear?

rows.text: After that, like a screw with stripped threads, that image was no longer bound to the darkness behind the closed door of our house.

groups.q: A boy plays soldier with his little brothers. Do his commands sound like real army drill?

rows.text: Battalion, forward march.
Beginning of stage one of the mission. Battalion, left turn.

groups.title: Poetry
groups.q: These are poems and lines of poetry: the narrator's own poem and lines by classical Persian poets (Kharaghani, Hafez, Attar). Does each one read as poetry in your language?

rows.text: My dreams were dark / I could see nothing / You came / The light of my dreams turned on / Now you are gone / The light of my dreams now blinks / I hold no hope of your return / But if your path should bring you near / come into my dreams one more time / I don't think my dreams believe you're gone / they think you are lost and
rows.note: the narrator's own simple poem to the girl he lost

rows.text: My dreams were dark / I could see nothing / You came / The light of my dreams ... the light of my dreams turned ... the light of my dreams turned on / Now ... now ... now you are gone ...
rows.note: he rehearses it half-asleep; the stumbling is on purpose

rows.text: One may write upon all things / except on water / and if you cross the sea / write upon the water with your own blood / so that the one who follows in your wake / will know that / lovers and / drunkards and / the burned ones / have passed this way.
rows.note: an old Persian poem by Kharaghani, written on a classroom board

rows.text: ... I would not take that signet ring of Solomon at any price, for now and then upon it the hand of ...
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; cut off as in the book

rows.text: I serve the Elder of the Tavern, whose grace ...
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; cut off as in the book

rows.text: The hope of union with you keeps me alive; or else my every breath, parted from you, would be the dread of death. … If you deal the wound, better that than another's balm, and if you give the poison, better that than ...
rows.note: two lines by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; the second is cut off as in the book

rows.text: ...Of Hafez's enchanting verse, only those are aware; those who know poetic grace and how to speak Persian.
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; cut off as in the book

rows.text: God unveiled the magnificent beauty of the divine face before the angels and saw they knew nothing of love; from that jealous zeal it turned to pure fire and struck the clay of Adam.
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet

rows.text: Remembering beloved and homeland, I will weep in such bitter grief, that from the world the road and custom of travel ...
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; cut off as in the book

rows.text: Long has it been since the beloved sent any message; no greeting written ...
rows.note: a line by Hafez, a classical Persian poet; cut off as in the book

rows.text: "For Attar, weeping till dawn is sweeter," or "now he lies more deeply slain"?
rows.note: a friend asks which of two songs; each is named by a line from a poem by Attar, a classical Persian poet

groups.title: Single words
groups.q: Under each line is one word from it and what it should mean. Is it the right word here?

rows.text: – You did the best thing, Nini-jan. They say newborns need a lot of sleep. Ten hours a day.
rows.note: "Nini" = loving family pet name for Mother

rows.text: – No peeking. If you peek, I'll sew you up.
rows.note: "I'll sew you up" = joking threat: I'll sew your eyes shut

rows.text: – Women? I wish he had. Whoever wants him can take him for herself. We'll throw something in on top.
rows.note: "We'll throw something in on top" = we'd even add something extra as a bonus

rows.text: – Sure, our Baba-jan really hungers for respect.
rows.note: "really hungers for respect" = badly craves respect (said sarcastically)

rows.text: – Yeah, right.
rows.note: "Yeah, right" = obviously yes, I was calling you

rows.text: – And then some.
rows.note: "And then some" = I fully agree, and even more

rows.text: – What a babe.
rows.note: "What a babe" = what a pretty girl (boy's slang)

rows.text: – No problem. I'll fight both of you at once, since you guys are both like little finches to me.
rows.note: "like little finches to me" = tiny and weak, easy to beat

rows.text: In a way, you could say they conquered the university. Karroubi is love, honestly and truly.
rows.note: "Karroubi is love" = Karroubi is great (excited youth slang)

rows.text: – Everything you do is a patch job.
rows.note: "a patch job" = sloppy makeshift fixes

rows.text: I press the elevator button. The elevator door opens. That day, Niloofar had come up the stairs. I go toward the stairwell. The voices of a boy and a girl drift out of the elevator. They call me sick.
rows.note: "sick" = nuts, a weirdo (said mockingly)

rows.text: – Can you explain what your relationship with your male relatives is like? Because I've heard that in Tehran ...
rows.note: "male relatives" = her boy cousins and young male kin

rows.text: Last year when he came, his wife's brothers had beaten him so badly, he was black all over.
rows.note: "black all over" = covered in bruises

rows.text: – Going into the main street: tsk-tsk.
rows.note: "tsk-tsk" = tongue click meaning no, forbidden

rows.text: – Yeah, I've heard a few things about this localization business.
rows.note: "localization" = regional quota system for university places

rows.text: – Yeah. Don't let this Arasteh fool you; goofy as he is, his Konkoor rank was seventy-four.
rows.note: "goofy as he is" = goofy, silly, said fondly

rows.text: A year or two ago I heard from Eagle Eye News that that dandy had gone to Australia too, sort of chasing the girl you both loved.
rows.note: "that dandy" = vain show-off, a dandy (mocking)

rows.text: – I know. I'm no dummy. But this won't work.
rows.note: "I'm no dummy" = I'm not stupid (said half annoyed)

rows.text: – And in that fucked-up situation, what antiques did we get stuck with?
rows.note: "antiques" = odd, weird people (mocking slang)

rows.text: – Leopard Farid, control your nerves and don't make a murderous move.
rows.note: "murderous move" = a rash, wild move (running joke)

rows.text: – Eagle Eye, God has already struck Fly; don't you strike him too. For your mother's sake, don't walk around the room without your glasses.
rows.note: "For your mother's sake" = a plea, I beg you; not an insult

rows.text: The important thing is that whenever I go to the supermarket, I pay money, buy my milk and cake, and put them in my body.
rows.note: "put them in my body" = eat them (blunt and funny)

rows.text: – Eldie, instead of sprawling on the bed like this and playing with your balls, get up and send them. It's a bargain.
rows.note: "It's a bargain" = a good deal; worth it

rows.text: – You're very sneaky.
rows.note: "You're very sneaky" = very sneaky (playful teasing)

rows.text: – You lot go stick to your jigily-jigily pop and Soosan Khanom. What business do you have listening to Moein?
rows.note: "jigily-jigily pop" = cheap bouncy pop (said with a sneer)

rows.text: – Kissing his ass doesn't suit you.
rows.note: "doesn't suit you" = sucking up isn't like you

rows.text: – Aaawwww. I was the one who told her that. Nini saw it was a good line and passed it on to you.
rows.note: "Aaawwww" = long, teasing, mock-tender 'aww'

rows.text: – I'd give anything for you, Nini-jan. Your mind works so well.
rows.note: "I'd give anything for you" = loving endearment: I'd give my life for you

rows.text: Now go get some seeds for Ghassem and the others. They want to watch a film.
rows.note: "seeds" = roasted seeds to snack on

rows.text: – He complains for no reason, heh, Amir-jan. If it isn't this, he'll find something else.
rows.note: "heh" = a short, soft laugh
